en: The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Spoken by Mañjuśrī*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhadra of Funan during the Liang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...
There was a great assembly of ten thousand bhikṣus; and there were also one hundred thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression.

Having long ago made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, they had planted deep roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas. They had brought sentient beings to maturity, purified Buddha-lands, attained dhāraṇīs, and acquired the eloquence of joyful speech. They had perfected wisdom and were endowed with merit. By means of their sovereign supernormal powers, they traveled through the worlds of various Buddhas, emitting immeasurable light and preaching inexhaustible, wondrous Dharma. They taught the bodhisattvas to enter the gate of the single characteristic, attained fearlessness, skillfully subdued the hosts of Māras, and converted and liberated those of external paths and heterodox views.

If there are sentient beings who delight in the vehicle of the śrāvakas, he teaches the śrāvaka-yāna; if they delight in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, he teaches the pratyekabuddha-yāna; if they delight in the worldly [vehicle], he teaches the worldly-yāna.

By means of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they gather in all sentient beings: those not yet crossed over, they cause to cross over; those not yet liberated, they cause to be liberated; those not yet at peace, they cause to find peace; and those not yet in *nirvāṇa*, they cause to attain *nirvāṇa*.
Having perfected the conduct of a bodhisattva, they have skillfully entered the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas.
They are fully endowed with all such various merits.
Their names are as follows:

The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha, the Bodhisattva Anikṣiptadhuravīrya, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta, the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, the Bodhisattva Sūryaviśuddha, the Bodhisattva Mahābala, the Bodhisattva Anantabala, the Bodhisattva Vīryaprāpta, the Bodhisattva Balaketudhvaja, the Bodhisattva Dharmaketu, and the Bodhisattva Vaśavartin.
Thus, one hundred thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as these,
together with the rest of the great assembly— including devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and others— all gathered there.

At that time, during the middle watch of the night, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance—blue, yellow, red, white, and the color of variegated crystal—which universally illuminated immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions.

All sentient beings who were touched by this light rose from their reclining positions; upon seeing this radiance, they all attained the joy of the Dharma and simultaneously gave rise to doubt, wondering:
"From where does this light come?"
"May the entire world cause all sentient beings to attain peace and happiness.
Having formed this thought,
from each and every ray of light there further issued forth great radiance, illuminating with extraordinary brilliance, surpassing the previous light, continuing thus in succession up to ten layers.

All the bodhisattvas, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, along with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, all leaped for joy, having attained what they had never experienced before.
Each of them thought to themselves:
"This must be the Tathāgata emitting this radiance; we should quickly go to where the Buddha is, to pay homage, draw near, and revere the Tathāgata."

At that time, Mañjuśrī and the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who encountered this light were filled with such joy and exultation that it pervaded their bodies and minds; each departed from their respective abodes and arrived at the gate of the Jeta Grove.
At that time, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākātyāyana, and Mahākauṣṭhila all went from their respective residences to the gate of the Jetavana.

Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and all the way up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, also beheld the radiance and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; together with their retinues, they brought exquisite celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial music, and celestial jewel-garments, and all arrived at the gate of the Jeta Grove.
The remaining bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as the eight classes of beings including devas and nāgas, were filled with joy upon encountering the light and all came to the gate.

At that time, the World-Honored One, possessing all-encompassing wisdom, knew that the entire great assembly was already outside the gate; he rose from his dwelling and went out to the gate, where he personally prepared the Dharma seat and sat down cross-legged.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"Did you come to the gate this morning?
Śāriputra replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Mañjuśrī and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have all already arrived.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī:
“Did you arrive at the gate first this morning?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha,
“It is so, World-Honored One!”

In the middle of the night, I beheld a great radiance shining in ten successive layers; having attained what I had never experienced before, my heart was filled with immeasurable joy and exultation. Therefore, I have come to pay homage and draw near to the Tathāgata, wishing also to hear the wondrous Dharma of the ambrosia.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī:
“Do you now truly see the Tathāgata?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One! The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is fundamentally invisible; it is for the sake of sentient beings that I have come to see the Buddha.

The Buddha’s Dharma-body is inconceivable: it is without marks and without form; it neither comes nor goes; it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is neither seen nor unseen; it is suchness and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); it neither departs nor arrives; it is neither non-being nor not non-being; it is neither a location nor not a location; it is neither one nor two; it is neither pure nor defiled; it is neither born nor extinguished.”
"My vision of the Tathāgata is also like this.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
"Do you now see the Tathāgata in such a way?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I truly have no seeing, nor do I have the characteristic of seeing.”
At that time, Śāriputra addressed Mañjuśrī:
"I do not now understand what you have said.
How is it that one thus perceives the Tathāgata?"
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra!
I do not perceive the Tathāgata in such a manner."
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī,
“What you have explained is utterly incomprehensible.
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
"That which is unresolvable is the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Prajñāpāramitā is neither resolvable nor unresolvable.
Śāriputra addressed Mañjuśrī:
"Do you give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward sentient beings?
Do you practice the six pāramitās for the sake of sentient beings?
Furthermore, do you enter nirvāṇa for the sake of sentient beings?"
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
“As you have said, I give rise to a mind of compassion for sentient beings, practice the six pāramitās, and enter into nirvāṇa;
yet sentient beings are in reality unobtainable—without marks, without form, neither increasing nor decreasing.”
Śāriputra! You have often thought thus:

"In each and every world there are Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who remain in the world for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, preaching each and every Dharma to teach, transform, and deliver sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, such that each and every sentient being attains parinirvāṇa."
"Do you have such a thought?
Śāriputra replied, "Mañjuśrī!..."
"I have always held this thought.
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
"As space is incalculable, so too are sentient beings incalculable; [the Buddha's wisdom] is likewise incalculable."
Space cannot be crossed over, nor can sentient beings be crossed over.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings are equal to space.
"How do the Buddhas teach and transform sentient beings? Śāriputra said,
"If all sentient beings are equal to empty space, for what reason do you preach the Dharma for sentient beings so that they may attain Bodhi?"
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
"Awakening is truly unattainable; what dharma should I then teach so that sentient beings might attain it?"
Why is this? Śāriputra, awakening and sentient beings are neither one nor two; they are without distinction and unconditioned, without name and without mark, truly non-existent.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from his *uṣṇīṣa*—a mark of a Great Man—a light of extraordinary and rare splendor, beyond all description.
It entered the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, and emerged again from his crown, universally illuminating the great assembly.
Having illuminated the great assembly, it then pervaded all worlds throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the great assembly was touched by this radiance; their bodies and minds experienced a bliss such as they had never before attained.
They all rose from their seats, gazed up at the World-Honored One and Mañjuśrī, and all thought to themselves:

"Today the Tathāgata has emitted this extraordinary and subtle light; it entered the crown of the crown prince Mañjuśrī’s head, emerged again from his crown, and shone universally upon the great assembly. Having illuminated the assembly, it then pervaded the ten directions."
"It is not without cause or condition that he will surely preach the sublime Dharma.
We should simply apply ourselves with diligent effort and take joy in practicing according to what has been taught.
Having reflected thus, they each addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That the Tathāgata has emitted this radiance today is not without cause or condition; he will surely proclaim the wondrous Dharma.
We look up to it with longing and desire to practice according to what is taught.”
Having made this request, he remained silent.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

The Tathāgata has emitted light and bestowed his supernatural power upon me; this light is rare and extraordinary, being neither color nor form, neither departing nor arriving, neither moving nor still, neither seen nor heard, and neither perceived nor known.
All sentient beings have nothing upon which to gaze, neither joy nor fear, and no conceptual discrimination.
I shall now, upholding the holy intent of the Buddha, expound this radiance so that all sentient beings may enter the wisdom of non-conceptualization.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"Excellent, excellent!
You have spoken most skillfully; I join you in your joy."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This radiance is the Prajñāpāramitā; the Prajñāpāramitā is the Tathāgata; and the Tathāgata is all sentient beings.”
“World-Honored One!
I cultivate the perfection of wisdom in this manner.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Good son! You have now spoken thus regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
I shall now question you: suppose someone were to ask you:”
"How many realms of sentient beings are there?
"How would you answer this?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If someone were to ask such a question, I would answer them:
‘The number of sentient beings is equal to the number of Tathāgatas.’”
“Mañjuśrī! If someone were to ask you again:
‘How vast or narrow is the realm of sentient beings?’”
"How would you answer?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If someone were to ask such a question, I would answer them:
'It is as vast or narrow as the realm of the Buddha. "Mañjuśrī!"
If you were further asked:
"In what place is the realm of sentient beings bound?
how would you answer?
“World-Honored One!
I would answer:
‘Just as the Tathāgata is bound, so too are sentient beings.’”
“Mañjuśrī! If someone were to ask you again:
‘Where does the realm of sentient beings abide?’”
"How should I answer?
"World-Honored One!
I would answer by saying:"
"Abiding in the realm of nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
"If you cultivate the prajñāpāramitā in this manner, does that prajñāpāramitā have a place of abiding?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā has no place of abiding.”
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“If the Prajñāpāramitā has no place of abiding, how do you cultivate it?
How do you study it?”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the prajñāpāramitā had a place of abiding, then there would be no cultivation or study.”
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“When you cultivate prajñā, do your roots of goodness increase or decrease?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
There are no roots of goodness that can be increased or decreased; if there were increase or decrease, it would not be the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
World-Honored One!”
To neither increase nor decrease the Dharma is to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
To neither abandon the dharmas of ordinary beings nor grasp at the dharmas of the Tathāgata is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
The perfection of wisdom is not cultivated for the sake of attaining dharmas, nor is it cultivated for the sake of not attaining dharmas.
One does not practice for the sake of practicing the Dharma, nor does one practice for the sake of not practicing the Dharma.
World-Honored One!
To neither gain nor abandon—this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? It is because it is not for the sake of the faults and afflictions of birth-and-death, nor for the sake of the merits of nirvāṇa,
World-Honored One!

If one cultivates the perfection of wisdom in this manner—neither grasping nor receiving, neither abandoning nor relinquishing, neither increasing nor decreasing, because of its non-arising and non-ceasing.
"Bhagavān!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should think thus:
'This dharma is superior, this dharma is middling, this dharma is inferior.'"
This is not the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Why? Because there are no dharmas that are superior, middling, or inferior.
“World-Honored One!
I cultivate the perfection of wisdom in this way.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“Are all Buddha-dharmas not supreme?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The Dharma of the Buddhas, the Dharma of Bodhisattvas, the Dharma of Śrāvakas, the Dharma of Pratyekabuddhas, and even the Dharma of ordinary beings—all these are unobtainable. Why is this?
Because it is ultimately empty.
Within ultimate emptiness, there are no dharmas of the Buddhas and no dharmas of ordinary beings.
Within the dharmas of ordinary beings, there is no ultimate emptiness.
"Why is this? Because neither emptiness nor non-emptiness can be apprehended.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Is the Buddha-dharma unsurpassed?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
There is not a single dharma, even as small as a mote of dust, that can be called "unsurpassed. Why is this?

Because the *dānapāramitā* is empty of *dānapāramitā*, and so on up to the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is empty of *prajñāpāramitā*; the ten powers (*daśabala*) are empty of the ten powers; the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), and even omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) are empty of omniscience.
In emptiness there is no unsurpassed, and in the unsurpassed there is no emptiness.
This is because both emptiness and non-emptiness are ultimately unapprehendable.
World-Honored One!
"The inconceivable dharma is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
"Do you not contemplate the Buddha-dharma?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If I were to contemplate the Buddha-dharma, I would see that the Buddha-dharma is unsurpassed.”
Why is this? Because there is no "unsurpassed" to be found,
World-Honored One.
The five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements are ultimately unobtainable, and all Buddha-dharmas are likewise unobtainable.
Within this state of unobtainability, there is neither that which can be obtained nor that which cannot be obtained.
"Bhagavān!
Within the Prajñāpāramitā, from ordinary beings up to the Buddhas, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma.
What dharma should I contemplate?"
The Buddha said:
"Good son! If there were no mental activity, you should not have said:..."
"One should not say, 'This is the dharma of ordinary persons,' or 'This is the dharma of pratyekabuddhas,' nor even say,
'This is the Buddha-dharma.'"
"Why is this? Because it cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!"
I have not, in truth, spoken of anything from the dharmas of ordinary persons up to the dharmas of the Buddhas. Why is this?
Because they do not cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha said:
"Good son, you also should not form such a thought:
"This is the desire realm, this is the form realm, this is the formless realm. Why is this?
Because they cannot be apprehended.
“World-Honored One!
The desire realm is empty of the nature of the desire realm, and so on, up to the formless realm being empty of the nature of the formless realm.
Within emptiness there is no speaking, and I likewise have nothing to say.”
World-Honored One!
When practicing the prajñāpāramitā, one perceives neither the superior nor the non-superior. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
In practicing the perfection of wisdom, one neither grasps at the Buddha-dharma nor abandons the dharma of ordinary beings. Why is this?
"Because in ultimate emptiness there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
"Excellent, excellent!"
That you are able to speak thus of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—this is the seal (*mudrā*) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Mañjuśrī!

If good sons or good daughters were not to have planted deep roots of goodness under thousands of millions of Buddhas, they would not hear this Dharma; rather, it is only by having planted deep roots of goodness under immeasurable and boundless Buddhas that one hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and gives rise to no fear.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Relying upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I shall further expound the profound Prajñāpāramitā.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent!
Listen as you please.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one does not perceive the arising of dharmas, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.”
Why is this? Because all phenomena are without arising.
If one does not apprehend the abiding of phenomena, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Why is this? Because all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*).
If one does not perceive cessation, that is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are quiescent.
"World-Honored One!..."
If one does not apprehend form, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; even unto not apprehending consciousness, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. Why is this?
"All dharmas are like illusions and like mirages.
"World-Honored One!
If one does not apprehend the eye, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; up to and including if one does not apprehend the mind, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom."

If one does not apprehend form, up to and including mental phenomena; if one does not apprehend the eye element, the form element, or the eye-consciousness element, up to and including the mental-object element or the mind-consciousness element—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
"If one does not apprehend the desire realm, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; it is the same even up to the formless realm.
'World-Honored One!

If one does not apprehend the perfection of giving, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; and so on, up to: if one does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.'"
If one does not attain the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, this is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this?
"Because of internal emptiness, and so on, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
World-Honored One!
If one perceives arising, abiding, and ceasing, this is not the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom."
If one perceives the five aggregates, the twelve bases, or the eighteen elements, one is not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
If one perceives the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, one is not practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If one attains anything from generosity (*dāna*) up to wisdom (*prajñā*), or if one attains anything from the ten powers (*bala*) of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), this is not the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Why is that?
"Because there is attainment.
World-Honored One!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is not startled, does not doubt, is not terrified, and does not retreat, one should know that this person has long planted roots of goodness under previous Buddhas."
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If one does not perceive defiled dharmas or pure dharmas; does not perceive the fruit of birth and death, nor the fruit of nirvāṇa; does not perceive a Buddha, nor a bodhisattva, nor a pratyekabuddha, nor a śrāvaka, nor an ordinary person—this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.”
Why is this? Because all dharmas are neither defiled nor pure, even to the extent that there are no ordinary beings.
World-Honored One!
World-Honored One, if one perceives defilement and purity, or even perceives ordinary beings, this is not the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*. World-Honored One,

if one perceives the differentiation of defiled phenomena, the differentiation of pure phenomena, or even the differentiation of Buddhas and the differentiation of ordinary beings' phenomena, this is not the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is without differentiation.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent!
This is the true practice of the prajñāpāramitā. Mañjuśrī!”
"How do you make offerings to the Buddha?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"If the mental activities of an illusory person were to cease, I would then make offerings to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
"Do you not abide in the Buddha-dharma?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
“The Buddha has no dharma in which to abide; how then could I abide?
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"If no dharma can be apprehended, who possesses the Buddha-dharma?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"There is no one who possesses the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
"Have you already reached the state of non-attachment?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
“Where there is no attachment, there is no arrival.
Why, World-Honored One, do you ask about having already arrived at non-attachment?”
The Buddha asked Mañjuśrī,
"Do you abide in bodhi?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Since even the Buddha does not abide in bodhi, how much less should I abide in bodhi?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Upon what do you rely to speak in this way?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
“I speak in this way without relying on anything.”
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“If you have no basis, what is it that you speak?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
I have nothing to say. Why is this?
"Because all dharmas are without names.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound Dharma, is not startled, doubtful, or terrified, will they certainly draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, upon hearing this profound Dharma, are not startled, doubtful, or terrified, will they draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
At that time, there was a goddess named Anālambanā who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this profound Dharma and is not startled, doubtful, or terrified, will they attain the Dharma of the śrāvakas, the Dharma of the pratyekabuddhas, the Dharma of the bodhisattvas, or the Dharma of the Buddhas?”
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
“So it is, so it is! Śāriputra!”
If any bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, upon hearing this profound Dharma, are not startled, doubtful, or terrified, they will certainly and surely attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

These good sons and good daughters shall become great donors, foremost donors, and supreme donors; they shall be fully endowed with morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; they shall be complete in all merits and achieve the marks and signs of excellence; they shall not themselves fear, nor cause others to fear; and they shall ultimately fulfill the *prajñāpāramitā*, because by means of the unobtainable, signless, and unconditioned, they achieve the foremost, inconceivable Dharma.
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
“What do you see? What do you delight in, that you seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Because I have neither view nor delight, I seek bodhi.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If there is neither seeing nor delight, there should likewise be no seeking.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
I truly have no seeking.
Why is this? Because whoever has seeking possesses the characteristic of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
The Buddha asked Mañjuśrī,
“Do you now truly not seek awakening?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha:
"I do not truly seek awakening.
Why is this? If one seeks awakening, that is the mark of an ordinary person."
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“Do you definitively seek, or do you definitively not seek?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:

"If one says that there is definite seeking, definite non-seeking, definite both seeking and non-seeking, or definite neither seeking nor non-seeking, these are the marks of an ordinary person. Why is this?"
“Because awakening has no place of abiding.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent!”

That you are able to speak thus of the *prajñāpāramitā* shows that you have already planted deep roots of merit under immeasurable Buddhas and have long practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*). All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice according to what you have said.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
“I have not planted roots of goodness, nor have I cultivated the holy life. Why is this?
If I plant roots of goodness, then all sentient beings shall also plant roots of goodness; if I cultivate the holy life, then all sentient beings shall also cultivate the holy life.
"Why is this? Because all sentient beings are the very mark of the brahmacarya.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"What have you seen, what have you realized, that you speak such words?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
"I have neither seen nor realized anything, nor is there anything for me to say."
World-Honored One!
I do not see ordinary persons, nor those in training, nor those beyond training, nor those who are neither in training nor beyond training.
Because I do not see them, I do not realize [them].
At that time, Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī,
"Do you see the Buddha?
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
"I do not even see śrāvakas, let alone see a Buddha. Why is this?
Because one does not perceive any dharmas, one is called a bodhisattva."
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī,
“Do you now definitively not perceive any dharmas?
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
“Venerable Great Bhikṣu!
Cease; you need not speak further.
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī:
"Who is it that speaks these words, 'He is called a Buddha'?
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
"Neither 'Buddha' nor 'non-Buddha' can be apprehended; there is no speaker and there is no one who teaches."
Śāriputra! Awakening cannot be expressed in words; how much less can there be a Buddha who can be spoken of or described?
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra!
You asked: "Of whom is this speech of the Buddha? This speech is neither joined nor dispersed;
it is neither born nor extinguished; it neither departs nor arrives. There is not a single dharma with which it can be associated; it is without letters and without phrases."
"Venerable Śāriputra!
Those who wish to see the Buddha should train themselves in this way.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What has been spoken by this Mañjuśrī cannot be understood by bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
"So it is, so it is! Venerable Śāriputra,
awakening is not something that can be understood."
"How should those who have newly resolved their minds understand this?
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī, "Do the Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas, not awaken to the dharma-realm?"
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
“Since even the Buddhas cannot be apprehended, how could there be a Buddha who awakens to the dharma-realm?
Śāriputra!...”
Since even the dharma-realm cannot be apprehended, how could the dharma-realm be that which is awakened to by the Buddhas? Śāriputra,
the dharma-realm is itself bodhi, and bodhi is itself the dharma-realm.
Why is this? Because all phenomena have no boundaries.
Venerable Śāriputra!

The dharma-realm and the Buddha’s sphere are without distinction; that which is without distinction is non-action; that which is non-action is the unconditioned; that which is unconditioned is beyond verbal expression; and that which is beyond verbal expression is non-existence.
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī,
“Are the entire dharma-realm and the sphere of the Buddha entirely non-existent?
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
"There is neither existence nor non-existence. Why is this?
Because existence and non-existence are of one mark, which is marklessness; they are neither one nor two."
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī,
“One who trains in this manner, will they attain bodhi?
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
"Training in this way, there is nothing to be trained in; one is not born in the happy realms nor does one fall into the evil destinies, one does not attain awakening nor enter nirvāṇa. Why is this?
Śāriputra! Because the Prajñāpāramitā is ultimately empty, within ultimate emptiness there is neither one, nor two, nor three, nor four; there is no coming or going, and it is inconceivable.
Venerable Śāriputra!
If one says, "I have attained bodhi," this is the speech of one with overweening pride (adhimāna). Why is that?

"Because they claim to have attained what they have not attained, such persons of overweening pride (adhimāna) are unworthy of receiving the faithful offerings of others; those with faith should not provide them with support.
Śāriputra addressed Mañjuśrī:
“What do you rely upon to speak in such a manner?
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
“I speak in this manner without relying on anything.”
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is equal to all dharmas.
All dharmas have no basis, because they are equal.
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī,
"Do you not use wisdom to eliminate and sever the afflictions?
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
"Are you an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted?
Śāriputra replied, "No."
Mañjuśrī said: "I, too, do not eliminate afflictions through wisdom.
Śāriputra said:
“Upon what basis do you speak thus, without fear or dread?
Mañjuśrī replied,
“Since even a self cannot be found, how could there be a self that would give rise to fear?”
Śāriputra said: “Excellent, Mañjuśrī!
You have most eloquently expounded such profound prajñāpāramitā.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī,
saying: "Good son,
are there bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, abiding in the bodhicitta, seek unsurpassed enlightenment?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
There is no bodhisattva who dwells in the bodhicitta while seeking unsurpassed enlightenment.”
Why is this? Because the bodhicitta cannot be apprehended, and unsurpassed enlightenment likewise cannot be apprehended.

The five crimes of immediate retribution are the very nature of bodhi; there is no bodhisattva who gives rise to a mind of immediate retribution to seek the fruit of such crimes. How, then, could there be a bodhisattva dwelling in the bodhicitta who seeks unsurpassed enlightenment through [the commission of] immediate retribution?
Bodhi is all dharmas. Why is this?
Because form and non-form cannot be apprehended, and so on, up to consciousness and non-consciousness, which likewise cannot be apprehended.

The eye is unattainable, and so on up to the mind being unattainable; forms are unattainable, and so on up to mental phenomena (*dharma*) being unattainable; the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the phenomenon-element (*dharmadhātu*) are also unattainable; birth is unattainable, and so on up to old age and death being unattainable; the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is unattainable, and so on up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) being unattainable; the ten powers of a Buddha are unattainable, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*) being unattainable.
The bodhicitta and unsurpassed enlightenment are both unobtainable; within that which is unobtainable, there is nothing to be obtained, nor is there anything unobtainable.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
"There is no bodhisattva who dwells in the bodhicitta seeking unsurpassed enlightenment.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
"Do you consider the Tathāgata to be your teacher?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have no thought that the Buddha is my teacher.
Why is this? Because...”
“World-Honored One!
Since even a self cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be a thought that says, ‘The Buddha is my teacher’?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Do you have any doubts regarding me?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
Since I do not even have certainty, how could there be doubt?
Why is this? Because one first attains certainty and only thereafter arises doubt.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“Do you not state definitively whether the Tathāgata is born?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha:
"If the Tathāgata were to arise, the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) would also have to arise. Why is this?
Because the dharma-realm and the Tathāgata are of one single characteristic and not two characteristics; for two characteristics cannot be found."
“Mañjuśrī! Do you believe that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, enter parinirvāṇa?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"All Buddhas are the very nature of nirvāṇa; that which is the nature of nirvāṇa neither enters nor does not enter.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"Do you say that the Buddhas undergo saṃsāra?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Even non-transmigration cannot be apprehended; how much less could transmigration ever be apprehended?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“The Tathāgata is without mind; this statement may be spoken only before a Tathāgata, or before Arhats whose outflows are exhausted, or before non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas.”
If other people were to hear these words, they would not give rise to faith, but would instead be startled and doubtful. Why is this?
Because this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, what kind of person is able to believe in this most profound Dharma?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“All ordinary beings are able to believe in this Dharma. Why is that?”
"The Tathāgata has no mind, for all ordinary beings likewise have no mind.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason do you speak this Dharma?
Both bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds and arhats all harbor doubts; we pray that you will explain it to us.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Within suchness, the true mark, the dharma-nature, the stability of dharmas, the fixed position of dharmas, and the limit of reality, is there any distinction between Buddhas and ordinary beings?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“If there is no distinction, why do you give rise to doubt?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Within non-differentiation, are there Buddhas and ordinary beings?
The Buddha said:
"There is! Why is this? Because the Buddha and ordinary beings are neither two nor distinct, for they share the single characteristic of being without characteristics."
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“Do you believe that the Tathāgata is the most supreme among all sentient beings?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I believe that the Tathāgata is the most supreme among all sentient beings.
World-Honored One!”
"If I were to believe that the Tathāgata is the most supreme among all sentient beings, then the Tathāgata would not be the most supreme.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
"Do you believe that the Tathāgata has accomplished all inconceivable dharmas?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I believe that the Tathāgata has accomplished all inconceivable dharmas.”
“World-Honored One!
If I were to believe that the Tathāgata accomplishes all inconceivable dharmas, then the Tathāgata would become conceivable.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Do you believe that all śrāvakas are those taught and transformed by the Tathāgata?
"World-Honored One!
I believe that all śrāvakas are those taught and transformed by the Tathāgata."
“World-Honored One!
If I were to believe that all śrāvakas are those taught and transformed by the Tathāgata, then the dharma-realm would become something that can be taught and transformed.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Do you believe that the Tathāgata is the unsurpassed field of merit?
"World-Honored One!
I believe that the Tathāgata is the unsurpassed field of merit."
World-Honored One!
If I were to believe that the Tathāgata is the unsurpassed field of merit,
then the Tathāgata would not be a field of merit.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“Upon what basis do you give me such an answer?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have answered thus without relying on anything.
World-Honored One!”

Within that which has no basis, there is neither superiority nor inferiority; there is nothing conceivable and nothing inconceivable; there is neither instruction nor non-instruction; there is neither a field of merit nor a non-field of merit.
At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, the earth shook in six ways.
A multitude of sixteen thousand bhikṣus attained liberation through the mind of non-apprehension;
seven hundred bhikṣuṇīs, three thousand upāsakas, and a multitude of forty thousand upāsikās were freed from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Sixty trillion nayutas of devas distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"For what cause and for what reason does this earth tremble so greatly?
At that time, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"This is because the Prajñāpāramitā is being expounded."
"In the past, all Buddhas have expounded this Dharma at this very place; for this reason, this earth quakes.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This which has been spoken by Mañjuśrī is inconceivable.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī:
"As Śāriputra has said, this which has been spoken by Mañjuśrī is indeed inconceivable."
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
That which is inconceivable cannot be spoken of; that which can be spoken of is conceivable."
"That which is inconceivable has no existence.
All those sounds are also inconceivable; that which is inconceivable has no sound.
The Buddha said:
“Have you entered the inconceivable samādhi?
Mañjuśrī replied, “No,
World-Honored One.”
I am indeed inconceivable; I do not perceive any mind capable of conceiving. How, then, can one say that I have entered the inconceivable samādhi?
When I first resolved to enter this concentration, I now reflect that, in reality, there is no characteristic of mind by which I enter samādhi.
It is like a person who practices archery: through long training, they become skilled.
Later, even though they have no conscious intent, because of their long practice, every arrow they release hits the mark.
I am also like this.
"When first learning the inconceivable samādhi, one binds the mind to a single object.
If, through long practice, it is accomplished, there is no further mental activity, and one is constantly in union with concentration.
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī:
"Is there any further, more excellent, subtle,
and tranquil meditative concentration? Mañjuśrī replied,
"If there were such an inconceivable concentration, you might ask about it."
"Is there yet another samādhi of tranquil extinction?
As I understand it, even an inconceivable samādhi cannot be found; how then can you ask me about a samādhi of tranquil extinction?
Śāriputra asked,
"Is the inconceivable samādhi unattainable?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Concentration that is conceivable has the characteristic of being attainable; concentration that is inconceivable has the characteristic of being unattainable.
All sentient beings truly possess this inconceivable concentration."
Why is this? Because all mental characteristics are themselves not mind; therefore, it is called the inconceivable samādhi.
For this reason, the characteristics of all sentient beings and the characteristics of the inconceivable samādhi are equal and without distinction.
The Buddha praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
You have long planted roots of goodness under various Buddhas and purely cultivated the Brahma-faring; thus you are able to expound this profound samādhi.”
"You now abide securely within this prajñāpāramitā.
Mañjuśrī said: "If I were to abide within prajñāpāramitā while being able to speak thus, that would constitute a conceptualization, and I would thereby abide in the notion of a self."
If one dwells within the perception of existence or the notion of a self, then the Prajñāpāramitā would have a location.
If the Prajñāpāramitā dwells in non-existence, that too is the notion of a self and is likewise called a location.
Departing from these two positions, one dwells in non-dwelling, abiding as all Buddhas abide—peacefully established in cessation, a realm beyond conceptual thought.
Such inconceivability is called the dwelling place of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
In the locus of the *prajñāpāramitā*, all phenomena are without marks (*animitta*), and all phenomena are without activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

The *prajñāpāramitā* is itself the inconceivable; the inconceivable is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); the dharma-realm is without marks; that which is without marks is the inconceivable; and the inconceivable is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The perfection of wisdom and the dharma-realm are non-dual and without distinction.
That which is non-dual and without distinction is the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm is signlessness; signlessness is the realm of the perfection of wisdom.
The realm of prajñāpāramitā is the inconceivable realm; the inconceivable realm is the realm of neither arising nor ceasing; and the realm of neither arising nor ceasing is the inconceivable realm.
Mañjuśrī said: "The realm of the Tathāgata and my own realm are of a non-dual nature.
One who practices the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner does not seek after bodhi."
Why is this? Because the characteristic of awakening is itself the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),
O Bhagavān.
If one knows the mark of self yet does not cling to it—this absence of knowledge and absence of clinging is what the Buddha knows.
This inconceivable absence of knowledge and absence of clinging is precisely what the Buddha knows.
Why is this? Because one knows that the essential nature of things has no marks of existence; how, then, could it transform the dharma-realm?
If one knows that the essential nature is without substance and without attachment, it is then called "non-entity."

If there is no entity, it is without location, without support, and without abiding; being without support and without abiding is itself non-arising and non-ceasing; and non-arising and non-ceasing is precisely conditioned merit.

If one knows in this way, then there is no mental conception. One who has no mental conception—how could they know the conditioned or unconditioned merits? This absence of knowing is the inconceivable.

That which is inconceivable is what the Buddha knows; it is neither grasping nor non-grasping. One does not perceive the marks of the three periods of time, such as going and coming, nor does one grasp at arising and ceasing or any formative activities. Furthermore, it is neither annihilated nor eternal. Knowing in this manner is called right knowledge and inconceivable knowledge.
"Just as space has neither 'this' nor 'that' and cannot be compared by analogy;
it has no good or evil, no equal or unequal, and is without marks or features," the Buddha told Mañjuśrī.
"If one knows in this way, it is called non-retrogressive wisdom.
Mañjuśrī said, "Non-conceptualizing wisdom is called non-retrogressive wisdom."
It is like a bar of gold: only after it has been subjected to hammering does one come to know its quality; if it were not treated by such forging, no one could discern it.

The characteristic of non-retrogressive wisdom is likewise so: it must be exercised within the sphere of experience, without thought or attachment, without arising or fabrication, fully unmoving, neither born nor ceasing—only then does it manifest.
At that time, the Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“Who would be able to believe the Tathāgatas when they speak of their own wisdom?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Such a wise person does not possess the dharma of nirvana, nor the dharma of saṃsāra; this is the practice of quiescence.
They do not sever greed, hatred, and delusion, yet it is not that they do not sever them."

Why is this? Because it is neither exhausted nor extinguished; it is neither separate from birth and death nor not separate from them; it is neither separate from the cultivation of the path nor not separate from the cultivation of the path.
One who forms such an understanding is said to possess right faith.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, “Excellent, excellent! It is as you have said;
you have profoundly understood this meaning.”
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Who in future ages will be able to believe in this profound Dharma?”
"Who would delight in hearing this Dharma?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"It is the fourfold assembly of today—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—who will be able to believe in this Dharma in future ages; upon hearing this profound Prajñāpāramitā being taught, they shall know this Dharma and seek this Dharma."
Kāśyapa!
It is like a householder or a householder’s son who has lost a great precious gem worth hundreds of millions of gold pieces, and thus experiences profound distress and affliction.
Now, having regained it once more, they give rise to great joy, and their distress is entirely extinguished.

In this same way, Kāśyapa, when bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās in future ages hear this most profound Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, which accords with Prajñā, they will experience joy upon hearing it; their minds will attain peace and happiness, and they will no longer have any further distress—just so it shall be.
One should speak thus:
"Today we have been able to see the Tathāgata and make offerings to the Tathāgata. Why is this so?"
"Because they have been able to hear this profound and subtle Dharma of the six pāramitās. "Kāśyapa,
it is like when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven see the first buds forming on the Pārijātaka tree, and they think thus:"
"This bud will surely blossom before long.
In the same way, Kāśyapa, when bhikṣus,
bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās hear this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, their hearts give rise to joy in just this manner.
"I shall certainly attain this Dharma in a future age. Kāśyapa!
This profound Prajñāpāramitā shall abide without perishing after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, circulating everywhere."
Kāśyapa! By the power of the Buddha, in future ages, if there are good sons or good daughters who shall obtain this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
“Kāśyapa! Just as a master of mani jewels feels joy upon seeing a mani gem and, without needing to deliberate, immediately knows whether it is genuine or counterfeit. Why is this?
Because they have seen this repeatedly.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!

If a person hears this Dharma associated with the Prajñāpāramitā and, having heard it, feels joy and gives rise to a mind of faith and delight, you should know that this person has already heard this Prajñāpāramitā in previous lives and has already made offerings to the Buddhas since time immemorial.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These good men and good women, having now heard this Dharma, will further develop faith and understanding in future ages.”
The Buddha told Mahākāśyapa:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said."
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma is without activity and without marks; he who expounds this Dharma is likewise without activity and without marks.”
"How is it, World-Honored One, that you speak of the characteristics of practice?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I cultivated all roots of goodness; desiring to abide in the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), one should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
Those who wish to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If good sons or good daughters wish to understand the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) and wish to know that the mental realms (*citta-dhātu*) of all sentient beings are entirely equal, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Mañjuśrī! Those who wish to study all Buddha-dharmas so as to achieve them fully and without obstruction should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Those who wish to study the infinite modes of conduct, the marks and signs, and the majestic deportment of all Buddhas at the time they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to know all the dharmas and modes of conduct by which all Buddhas do not fail to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because within these dharmas of emptiness, one does not perceive the *bodhi* of the Buddhas and so forth.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to know such characteristics without doubt or confusion, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because in the Prajñāpāramitā, one does not perceive any phenomena as arising or ceasing, nor as defiled or pure.
Therefore, sons and daughters of good family should train in the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner.
If one wishes to know that all phenomena lack the characteristics of past, future, and present, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) are devoid of past, future, and present.
If one wishes to know that all phenomena enter equally into the dharma-realm with a mind free from obstruction, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to attain the wheel of Dharma of three turnings and twelve aspects, and likewise personally realize it without grasping or attachment, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to attain a mind of loving-kindness that pervades all sentient beings without limit or partiality, yet does not form the notion of a mark of "sentient being," one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to never give rise to contentious debate regarding any sentient being, nor even to grasp at the mark of "non-contention," one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to know what is possible and what is impossible, the ten powers, and the fearlessnesses; to abide in the wisdom of a Buddha and attain unimpeded eloquence, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

When I contemplate the True Dharma, it is unconditioned and signless; there is no attainment and no benefit, no arising and no ceasing, no going and no coming. There is no knower, no seer, and no doer. One does not perceive the Prajñāpāramitā, nor does one perceive the sphere of the Prajñāpāramitā. It is neither realization nor non-realization; it is free from conceptual proliferation and devoid of discrimination.”

All dharmas are inexhaustible and free from exhaustion; there is no dharma of ordinary beings, no dharma of śrāvakas, no dharma of pratyekabuddhas, and no dharma of buddhas. They are neither attained nor unattained, neither abandoning saṃsāra nor realizing nirvāṇa, neither conceivable nor inconceivable, and neither created nor uncreated.
“Since the characteristics of dharmas are thus,
how should one study the Prajñāpāramitā?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"If one can thus know the characteristics of all dharmas, this is called training in the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to train in the *bodhy-vaśitā-samādhi*, and having attained this samādhi, illuminates all profound Buddha-dharmas, knows the names of all Buddhas, and also fully understands all Buddha-worlds without obstruction, they should train in the *prajñāpāramitā* as taught by Mañjuśrī."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason is it called ‘prajñāpāramitā’?”
The Buddha said: “The Prajñāpāramitā is boundless and limitless; it is without name and without mark, beyond conceptualization.

It has no refuge and no island; it is without transgression and without merit, without darkness and without light. Like the dharma-realm, it has no boundaries and no finite measure. This is called the Prajñāpāramitā, and it is also called the sphere of practice for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.”
The state that is neither practice nor non-practice fully enters the One Vehicle; it is called the "state of non-practice. Why is this?
Because it is without thought and without action.
This is the mother of all Buddhas, for it is from this that all Buddhas are born.
Why is this? Because it is unborn.
"Therefore, Mañjuśrī, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to practice the bodhisattva conduct and fulfill all the pāramitās, they should cultivate this prajñāpāramitā."
If one wishes to sit upon the seat of enlightenment and attain unsurpassed bodhi, one should cultivate this Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to universally encompass all sentient beings with great loving-kindness and great compassion, one should cultivate this Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to give rise to the skillful means for all meditative concentrations, one should cultivate this Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to attain all samāpattis, one should cultivate this Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because all samādhis have no objective purpose.
All dharmas neither transcend nor possess a place of transcendence; if a person wishes to follow this teaching, they should cultivate the prajñāpāramitā.
All dharmas are, in accordance with reality, unattainable; if one wishes to know them thus, one should practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

All sentient beings cultivate the path to enlightenment for the sake of bodhi, yet in truth there are no sentient beings and no bodhi; if a person wishes to have faith and delight in this dharma, they should practice the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are, in their true nature, equal to bodhi.

They are not the conduct of sentient beings, nor do they abandon their own nature. That which is the conduct of sentient beings is non-conduct; that non-conduct is bodhi; and that bodhi is the dharma-realm.
"If one wishes not to be attached to this Dharma, one should cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā. Mañjuśrī!

If a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā receives and maintains even a single four-line verse of the Prajñāpāramitā and explains it to others, I say that such a person attains the state of non-falling; how much more so for those who practice according to reality."
"You should know that those sons and daughters of good family abide in the realm of the Buddha. Mañjuśrī!
If sons and daughters of good family, upon hearing this profound Prajñāpāramitā, do not give rise to fear,"
You should know that this person has received the seal of the Buddha-dharma.
This Dharma-seal was created by the Buddha and is held in high esteem by the Buddha. Why is this so?
Because this Dharma-seal seals the dharma of non-attachment.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family is sealed by this seal, you should know that such a person follows the Bodhisattva vehicle and is certain not to regress, nor will they fall into the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.

At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra and the various sons of the gods, from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, rained down fine powdered sandalwood and fine powdered gold dust; they also scattered blue utpala flowers, red padma flowers, yellow kumuda flowers, white puṇḍarīka flowers, and māndārava flowers as an offering to the Prajñāpāramitā.
Having made the offering, he spoke these words:
"I have already made offerings to the unsurpassed, unattached, and most supreme Dharma; may I, in future lives, further hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā."

If a person has already been sealed with this seal of the profound Prajñāpāramitā, may they, in the future, again obtain its hearing and reception, ultimately accomplishing the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñajñāna).
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this Prajñāpāramitā even once enter their ears, for the sake of increasing the Buddha-dharma, I shall protect that person within a hundred yojanas so that non-human beings may find no opportunity to harm them.”
"These sons and daughters of good family shall ultimately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
I shall go to their abodes every day to present offerings."
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra Devānām-indra:
“So it is, so it is! Kausika!”
It should be known that those sons and daughters of good family, being fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma, will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha,
saying: "I only pray, World-Honored One,
that by your majestic spiritual power you will sustain this Prajñāpāramitā so that it may abide long in the world, for the sake of bringing benefit and joy to all sentient beings."
When Mañjuśrī had spoken these words, by the supernatural power of the Buddha, the great earth shook in six ways.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled and emitted a great radiance that illuminated the entire trichiliocosm; through his majestic spiritual power, he sustained this Prajñāpāramitā so that it might long abide in the world.
At that time, Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Is the emission of this radiance a sign of upholding the Prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “So it is, so it is! Mañjuśrī!”
I emit this light; it is the mark of upholding the Prajñāpāramitā. Mañjuśrī!
You should know now that I have upheld this Prajñāpāramitā for a long time in the world.
If there is anyone who does not disparage this Dharma and does not speak of its faults, one should know that this person has already been sealed with the seal of this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī! I have dwelt for a long time in this seal;
if a person has been sealed by this seal, you should know that such a person cannot be taken advantage of by the Māra-king.
The Buddha told Śakra:
"You should receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and widely proclaim and disseminate it, so that all good sons and good daughters in future ages may obtain this Dharma-seal."
He further addressed Ānanda:
"You, too, should receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it extensively for others.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Elder Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named?
How should we receive and uphold it?”
The Buddha said:
"This sutra is named 'Expounded by Mañjuśrī,' and it is also named 'Prajñāpāramitā'; you should receive and uphold it thus."

If a son or daughter of good family, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were to bestow priceless jeweled pearls upon sentient beings equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, and those beings, having received them, all gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; at that time, the donor would provide instruction, admonition, benefit, and joy according to what was appropriate for each, causing them to attain the fruit of Srotāpanna up to the fruit of Arhat.
"Would the merit obtained by this person be great?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
"It would be very great, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said, "Good son!

If a person gives rise to even a single thought of faith in this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and does not slander it, their merit exceeds that of the former by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-ten-thousand-millionfold, and even beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy; how much more so for one who fully receives, maintains, recites, and explains it to others!"
The merit obtained by such a person is immeasurable and boundless; all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, cannot exhaustively describe it.
Why is this? Because it gives birth to the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) of all Buddhas.

If space were to come to an end, then the merit of this sutra would come to an end; if the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) were to come to an end, then the merit of this sutra would come to an end. Therefore, Mañjuśrī!
Good sons and good daughters, you should diligently practice vigor to protect this sutra.

This sutra can extinguish all fears of birth and death, can topple the supreme banners erected by the heavenly Māras, can lead Bodhisattvas to the fruit of Nirvāṇa, and instructs and guides them to remain apart from the two vehicles.
At that time, Śakra and the Elder Ānanda both addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! It is so, it is so!”
"Just as the Buddha has spoken, we shall receive and uphold it upon our heads and propagate it widely.
We only pray that the Tathāgata will not worry.
Thus they spoke three times.
“Please do not worry; we shall receive and uphold this with the highest reverence.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Mañjuśrī and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, Śāriputra and the other bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as the entire assembly of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced and faithfully accepted and upheld it.
In the *Mañjuśrī-bhāṣita-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Have you entered the inconceivable samādhi?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha:
"No, World-Honored One!
If I were to enter an inconceivable concentration, I would then become conceivable.
World-Honored One!"
"With a mind that is no-mind, how shall I enter the inconceivable samādhi?
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when I first resolved upon the aspiration for bodhicitta, I said:"
"I shall enter the inconceivable samādhi"—
I do not now have this intention that I shall enter the inconceivable samādhi,
World-Honored One!
It is like a beginner learning archery who first forms this intention:
"I shall shoot at the target.
Once the shooting of the target is accomplished, he later forms this thought:
"I shall shoot the hide.
Having succeeded in shooting the hide, he further thought:
"I shall shoot the wood."
Once he had mastered shooting at wood, he further thought:
"I shall shoot at iron.
Having mastered shooting at iron, he no longer harbored his former thoughts; wherever his arrows struck, they were all able to pass right through.
I am also like this.
In the past, when I first resolved my mind, I sought to enter the inconceivable samādhi.
Today, I no longer have such an intention; I shall instead enter the inconceivable samādhi.
"Why is this? Because this samādhi is inconceivable.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Mañjuśrī should not yet have attained abiding. Why is this?
"Apart from this inconceivable samādhi, there is yet another tranquil samādhi, for that is what he ought to attain.
Mañjuśrī said to Śāriputra,
"How do you know that apart from this inconceivable samādhi there is yet another tranquil samādhi?"
"Venerable Śāriputra!
If this inconceivable concentration could be attained, then there might be a concentration of tranquility apart from this concentration.
If this inconceivable concentration cannot be attained, then that concentration of tranquility likewise cannot be attained."
Why is this? Because this inconceivable samādhi cannot be apprehended, that [subject] likewise cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra!
There is no sentient being who does not attain this samādhi; all sentient beings attain this samādhi. Why is this?
Because all minds are, in their essence, mindless.
That which is the absence of a mind-nature is itself this samādhi; therefore, all sentient beings attain this samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent!”
What you have said is the most supreme meaning.
You have planted deep roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas throughout the distant past, and thus you are able to speak in this way, Mañjuśrī!
Do you have this thought:
"Abiding in the perfection of wisdom, I am able to speak these words"? No?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“No, World-Honored One!
I have no such thought.”
"Bhagavān! If I were to have this thought:
'Abiding in the prajñāpāramitā, I am able to speak these words,' then I would be abiding in a dharma that can be apprehended."
“World-Honored One!
If I were to abide in the mark of a self, then such a thought would arise.
Therefore, World-Honored One!”
"I did not have this thought:
'Abiding in the Prajñāpāramitā, one is able to speak these words.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
“Who will believe what you say?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
If a person does not cling to the characteristics of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, that person believes what I have taught.
Furthermore, if a person stubbornly clings to a self, or if a person is possessed of the three poisons, such a person cannot believe.
"Why is this? Because views and afflictions are not subject to extinction.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent!
You have spoken well.
Noble sons and noble daughters, as for the characteristics of practice, they consist in believing this Dharma and upholding this Dharma.”
Because of the mind of non-apprehension, practice is also non-apprehensible, and characteristics are also non-apprehensible. Mañjuśrī!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family delights in this non-apprehension, they should listen to this Prajñāpāramitā.
If good sons or good daughters wish to attain the stage of non-retrogression, they should listen to this Prajñāpāramitā.
If good sons or good daughters wish to have faith that all dharmas are equal to the dharma-realm, they should listen to this Prajñāpāramitā.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to know all dharmas, they should listen to this Prajñāpāramitā.
If a person attains faith in this meaning, they should listen to this Prajñāpāramitā.
If a person does not delight in contemplating all dharmas, they should listen to the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
Because in this Prajñāpāramitā, no dharmas are perceived.
Mañjuśrī! If a son or daughter of good family wishes to know that all dharmas are neither impure nor defiled, they should listen to this Prajñāpāramitā.
If good sons or good daughters wish to attain freedom from doubt, they should listen to this Prajñāpāramitā.

If good sons or good daughters wish to cover all sentient beings with impartial compassion, to abide in no mark of a sentient being, and not to contend with the world, they should listen to this Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One!

The Prajñāpāramitā is without self and without what belongs to a self; it is without arising and without ceasing; it is without cause and without fruit; it is without anything to be grasped or maintained. How can one receive and uphold it so as to obtain merit?"

The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “The Prajñāpāramitā is without creation and without cessation; it is neither the dharma of ordinary beings nor the dharma of noble ones; it is neither the dharma of saṃsāra nor the dharma of transcending saṃsāra; it is neither the dharma of nirvāṇa nor the dharma of transcending nirvāṇa; it is without gain and without loss; it is neither conceivable nor inconceivable.”

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family listens and receives [this teaching] in this way, they will be in accord with the Prajñāpāramitā; this is merit, yet it is also the absence of merit.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the bodhisattva samādhi, wishes to know the names of all buddhas, wishes to see all buddha-worlds, wishes to hear the Dharma taught by all buddhas, and wishes to practice the teachings of all buddhas, they should study this Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is it called ‘prajñāpāramitā’?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “The Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable and boundless;
it has no direction and no location; it neither goes nor comes; it is without action and unconditioned. It is the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas; therefore, it is named Prajñāpāramitā.”
Mañjuśrī! This Prajñāpāramitā is the sphere of practice for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; because bodhisattvas practice within this sphere, it is called their "sphere of practice."
Why is this? Because there is no location."
